title: Spacing: the same practice, spread out, and how far apart

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-09-25.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Spacing, which Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) call distributed practice, is a schedule: the same material is studied or retrieved on two or more occasions spread out in time. Massed practice, often called cramming, puts the same occasions back to back.

The gap is the time between two study sessions of the same material. The retention interval, from section 1, is the time from the last study session to the test.

The spacing effect is the finding that, for the same total study time, spaced practice gives better long-term retention than massed practice.

Cepeda and colleagues (2008) taught 1,354 people 32 trivia facts. Their numbers here are from the authors’ manuscript. Final recall first rose as the gap grew, then fell. Of the gaps tested, the best were 1, 11, 21 and 21 days for retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days.

As shares of the retention interval, those best gaps were 14%, 31%, 30% and 6%. They are rough, because only six or seven gaps were tried. The abstract rounds them to about 20% for a test a few weeks away and about 5% for a year. The authors’ fitted curve smooths them into a best gap that grows while its share falls. This book uses 20% to 30% as a planning window for tests a few weeks away.

Overall, recall at the best gap was 64% higher than with no gap: a relative increase, not percentage points. By retention interval it ran from 10% for a test a week away to 111% for 70 days. A gap longer than the best cost less than a gap shorter than the best.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Take the same three hours of study. Spend them in one evening, or spread them over three weeks. The spread-out hours leave more behind a month later.

It does not feel that way. Straight after a cramming session, you remember a lot, and on a test that day cramming can win.

Say the test is a few weeks away. This book suggests a gap before the review about 20% to 30% as long as the wait from the review to the test. That window comes from one large study of facts. Treat it as a starting point, and if you are unsure, err on the long side.

Make the review a retrieval, not a reread (section 3): close the book, write what you remember, then check.

blocks.alt: Four separate points: gap 1 day at 7 days, 11 at 35, 21 at 70, and 21 at 350. A straight line for 20% of the retention interval rises steeply to 70 at 350 days; a dashed line for 5% rises gently and passes just below the last point.
blocks.caption: Cepeda and colleagues (2008), recall: the best of the gaps tested was 1, 11, 21 and 21 days for retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days. The two straight lines are a gap of 20% and of 5% of the retention interval. The points for 35 and 70 days sit above the 20% line, the 7-day point just below it, and the 350-day point near the 5% line. The points are the best of the few gaps tried, so nothing is drawn between them.

blocks.alt: Two pairs of bars. At a 20% gap: gap 7 days, retention interval 35. At a 30% gap: gap 9.69, retention interval 32.31. A horizontal dashed line at 11 days.
blocks.caption: The worked calendar example: 42 days from teaching to test, split into the gap before the review and the retention interval after it. A gap of 20% of the retention interval puts the review on day 7, leaving 35 days; a gap of 30% puts it on day 9.69, leaving 32.31. Each pair adds up to the whole 42. The dashed line is the best gap Cepeda tested for a 35-day retention interval, 11 days.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Here is the plan most of us were taught by. Cover a topic in one week of the course. Revise it all in the week before the examination. Every revision session goes well, because you have only just seen the material. That good feeling is the trap.

Open Dunlosky and colleagues, “Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques”, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 2013, at https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266, and go to section 9, Distributed practice. It describes an old experiment. Students learned Spanish words, then relearned them in six more sessions. The sessions were back to back, 1 day apart, or 30 days apart. With 30 days between sessions, students forgot the most in between, and they never caught up with the others during practice. Search for 30 days later.

the pattern reversed on the final test 30 days later, such that the best retention of the translations was observed in the condition in which relearning sessions had been separated by 30 days.

The schedule that looked worst during practice was best a month later. Read on.

the condition with the most intersession forgetting yielded the greatest long-term retention.

Why spacing works is debated. One account is that a review soon after learning is too easy to do much work. Cepeda and colleagues doubt it fits gaps of days and weeks.

So how far apart should the sessions be? Open Cepeda and colleagues, “Spacing effects in learning: a temporal ridgeline of optimal retention”, Psychological Science 2008. The copy free to read is the authors’ own manuscript, at https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED505660.pdf. Its first line warns that it “may differ from the final published version”.

Each learner studied the facts, waited a gap, went through them once more by answering each question and then seeing the answer, waited a retention interval, and took a final test. RI is the paper’s short form for retention interval. Search for respectively.

For the RIs of 7, 35, 70, and 350 days, the optimal gaps (of those included in the study) were 1, 11, 21, and 21 days, respectively, for recall data

Divide each best gap by its retention interval. That is a ratio of two times in the same unit (Book 0, A5), and 100 times it is a percentage (Book 0, A4).

1 divided by 7 = 0.1428571429
11 divided by 35 = 0.3142857143
21 divided by 70 = 0.3
21 divided by 350 = 0.06

Multiplied by 100 and rounded: 14%, 31%, 30% and 6%.

retention interval (days) best gap tested (days) gap as % of retention interval
7 1 14
35 11 31
70 21 30
350 21 6

For a test a year away, the best gap tested was 6% of the retention interval, not 30%.

The authors also fitted one smooth surface to all 26 conditions. Search for 23 days.

the optimal gap for RI = 350 equals 23 days, which is just 7% of the RI.

On that surface the best gap grows as the test moves away, while its share falls. That shape was one of the constraints the authors built the surface to meet.

Their abstract rounds the shares off: about 20% for a test a few weeks away, falling to about 5%, or 0.05, for a test a year away. Last, search for too small a gap.

while there are costs to using a gap that is longer than the optimal value, these costs are much smaller than the costs of using too small a gap value

Too long is the cheaper mistake.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The best gaps in the table are the best of a few tried: six or seven gaps at each retention interval. The real best can sit anywhere between two tried gaps. That is why the share jumps from 14% to 31% and back down to 6%. Read the shares as rough, not exact.

These were adults of many ages and countries, learning trivia facts online, with one review, tested up to 350 days later. For a test years away, for a skill, or for a large body of connected material, the numbers are a guess carried past the data.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now put it on a calendar. On Monday 5 October 2026 you teach a batch of MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery) students how to plot a child’s weight on a growth chart. Their test is on Monday 16 November, 42 days later. There is room for one review in class. When should it go?

The 42 days are the gap plus the retention interval. For a test a few weeks away, use this book’s planning window: a gap of about 20% to 30% of the retention interval. Work out both ends.

At 20%, the gap is 0.2 times the retention interval. So the whole 42 days is 1 times the retention interval plus 0.2 times it, which is 1.2 times it. Divide to undo the multiplication (Book 0, C2).

42 divided by 1.2 = 35
0.2 times 35 = 7
7 plus 35 = 42

At 30%, the whole is 1.3 times the retention interval.

42 divided by 1.3 = 32.31
0.3 times 32.31 = 9.69

The review goes on day 7 to day 10 after teaching. Count forward from 5 October: day 7 is Monday 12 October, and day 10 is Thursday 15 October. If the timetable gives you a choice, take the later day, because too long is the cheaper mistake. Check it against the data: for a 35-day retention interval, the best gap tested was 11 days. Day 10 sits close to it.

Make the review a retrieval (section 3). Each student, alone, writes the steps of plotting the chart from memory, then you show the answer. Weinstein and colleagues note that spacing costs little if you “set aside a few minutes per class to review information from previous lessons”.

Do the same for yourself. You will teach the topic to residents without notes on Monday 30 November. You study it on Monday 2 November: 28 days before.

28 divided by 1.2 = 23.3
0.2 times 23.3 = 4.66
28 divided by 1.3 = 21.5
0.3 times 21.5 = 6.45

Round 4.66 up to 5, since too long is the cheaper mistake. Review on day 5 or day 6: Saturday 7 or Sunday 8 November. Close the book, write out what you would teach, and only then open it to check.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The 20% to 30% is a rough figure for tests a few weeks away. It comes from one study of trivia facts with a single review. It gives you a window for a date, not a measured best day for your topic.

For an examination months or years away, the share is smaller, and the data stop at 350 days. That study did not compare one review with several. Add later reviews if you can, but no figure here says how far apart they should be.

points.html: “Three hours is three hours, however you spread them” is the error. With study time held equal, spaced practice leaves more behind on a delayed test.
Never judge a schedule by how the practice sessions go.
Before you pick a review date, write down when the learning must be used: the test date, or the day you will teach it. Then set the gap from that.

Do not plan a long interval with a fixed share. Dunlosky and colleagues summarise Cepeda and colleagues’ study as a fixed “10 to 20%” of the retention interval. On the authors’ fitted curve the share falls: 23 days, 7%, for a test 350 days away (21 days was the best they tried).
When you are unsure of the best gap, choose the longer one.

Test often and lightly, so that students space their own study. In one study, when tests came only every 3 weeks, students left their study until just before each test. With daily tests, their study was spread out.
These gaps were measured for trivia facts, one review and tests up to 350 days away. Past a year, treat any gap figure as a starting guess. Then check it with a delayed test of your own (section 2).

blocks.prompt: Pick a topic you will teach in the next month, to MBBS students, residents or accredited social health activists. Write down the date you teach it and the date it must be used: a test, a posting or a field visit. Then set the date of one in-class review, show the arithmetic, and say what the learners will do at the review. Finally, set your own review date if you will teach the topic from memory.
blocks.answer:
A good plan names the two end dates first. Everything else is worked out from them.

It splits the days between them into a gap and a retention interval. For an end date a few weeks away, the gap is about 20% to 30% of the retention interval. So the whole is 1.2 to 1.3 times the retention interval. Dividing gives a window of days, not a single day, and the plan picks the later end when it can.

At the review, each learner retrieves alone and without notes, and then sees the answer (section 3). Rereading the notes together is not the review this evidence supports.

Your own review follows the same arithmetic, counted back from the day you teach. The end date may be many months away. Then the plan says the share should be smaller, and that no figure here was measured for that distance.

blocks.prompt: You have ten minutes and a whiteboard with a first-year resident. She asks: “Why not teach each topic once and do a full revision week before the exam? It works for me.” Explain the mechanism and the evidence, and what you would change in her plan.
blocks.answer:
Start from her experience, because it is real. Revision just before an exam does feel like it works, and on a test straight after, cramming can do as well or better.

Then draw the two schedules on the board. One: topic, a long empty stretch, a revision week, the exam. Two: topic, a short review a week or two later, and the exam. Say what the evidence measured: with the same study time, the spread-out schedule leaves more behind on a delayed test. In one large study, recall after the best gap was 64% higher than after no gap, from 10% to 111% depending on when the test came.

Explain why it feels wrong. A review soon after learning is easy, so it feels productive. A review after some forgetting is harder. Weinstein and colleagues call this a “desirable difficulty”: harder now, better later. Say that why it works is still debated. The schedule with the most forgetting between sessions did best a month later.

Then change the plan. Decide when each topic must be used. Put one review so that the gap before it is about 20% to 30% as long as the wait after it. Make it a closed-book attempt, with the answers checked after. Keep a revision week if she likes, as a second review, not the only one.

blocks.prompt: Write each ratio as a percentage, to the nearest whole number: 11 divided by 35, then 21 divided by 350, then 23 divided by 350.

blocks.answer:
Turn each percentage into a decimal by dividing by 100, then multiply.

20 divided by 100 = 0.2
0.2 times 45 = 9
5 divided by 100 = 0.05
0.05 times 360 = 18

9 and 18.

blocks.prompt: Split 36 into two parts. The smaller part must be 0.2 times the larger part. Find both parts.
blocks.answer:
The whole is the larger part plus 0.2 times the larger part, which is 1.2 times the larger part. Divide the whole by 1.2 to get the larger part.

36 divided by 1.2 = 30
0.2 times 30 = 6
30 plus 6 = 36

The parts are 30 and 6.

blocks.prompt: Cepeda and colleagues (2008) also gave a multiple-choice recognition test. For retention intervals of 7, 35, 70 and 350 days, the best gaps tested for recognition were 1, 7, 7 and 21 days. Work out each best gap as a percentage of its retention interval, to the nearest whole number. Say which way the percentage moves as the retention interval grows. Then compare the gaps with the recall gaps of 1, 11, 21 and 21 days.
blocks.answer:
Divide each gap by its retention interval, then multiply by 100.

1 divided by 7 = 0.1428571429
7 divided by 35 = 0.2
7 divided by 70 = 0.1
21 divided by 350 = 0.06

14%, 20%, 10% and 6%. The share does not fall at every step: it rises from 14% to 20% between 7 and 35 days, then falls to 10% and 6%. The gaps tested were coarse, so one step up is not a pattern.

For recognition, the best gaps at 35 and 70 days were 7 days, against 11 and 21 days for recall. The best gap depended on the kind of test as well as on its date. A choice-of-answers test and a write-it-out test are different targets.

blocks.prompt: You teach a batch of MBBS students a topic on 1 December 2026. Their test is 60 days later. Take the gap as 20% to 30% of the retention interval, this book’s planning window for a test some weeks away. Work out the test date, and the range of days after teaching on which the one review should fall, with its dates.
blocks.answer:
The test date first. December has 31 days.

1 plus 60 = 61
61 minus 31 = 30

Day 60 is 30 January 2027.

The 60 days are the gap plus the retention interval. At 20%, the whole is 1.2 times the retention interval.

60 divided by 1.2 = 50
0.2 times 50 = 10

At 30%, the whole is 1.3 times the retention interval.

60 divided by 1.3 = 46.15
0.3 times 46.15 = 13.85

The review goes on day 10 to day 14 after teaching.

1 plus 10 = 11
1 plus 14 = 15

From 11 December to 15 December 2026. If you must pick one day, pick the later one: a gap too long costs less than one too short.

blocks.prompt: The timetable fixes your one review 9 days after you first teach a topic. You want the gap to be 20% to 30% of the retention interval. How many days after the review should the test fall, and how many days after the first teaching is that?
blocks.answer:
This time the gap is known and the retention interval is not. The gap is the share times the retention interval, so the retention interval is the gap divided by the share.

9 divided by 0.3 = 30
9 divided by 0.2 = 45

A larger share gives a shorter retention interval. The test should fall 30 to 45 days after the review. Add the 9 days of the gap.

9 plus 30 = 39
9 plus 45 = 54

39 to 54 days after the first teaching. A test much sooner than that makes the 9-day gap too long for it. As Cepeda and colleagues found, that is the cheaper mistake, but it is still a mistake.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Cepeda and colleagues: the best gap gave a 64% increase in final recall over no gap
suppose recall with no gap was 40%
40 plus 64 = 104
104% recall is impossible, so the 64% figure must be wrong

The 40% is made up for the sake of the sum. The paper’s recall scores for each condition are in a figure this book does not hold.
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the third. A 64% increase is a per cent change, not a gain of 64 percentage points (Book 0, A4). It means the new value is the old value plus 64% of the old value.

0.64 times 40 = 25.6
40 plus 25.6 = 65.6

65.6%, which is possible. The same figure can also be written as 1.64 times 40.

1.64 times 40 = 65.6

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. Both numbers carry a percent sign, and adding two percentages feels natural. But one is a share of the facts recalled and the other is a change relative to a starting value. They cannot be added.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a student’s worked plan. Find the step that broke.

I start the topic on 20 October; the exam is 30 days later, on 19 November
the gap should be 20% of the time
20% of 30 days = 6 days
so I revise 6 days before the exam, on 13 November
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the last. The gap is the time from first study to the review, not from the review to the exam. Revising 6 days before the exam makes the gap 24 days and the retention interval 6 days.

30 minus 6 = 24
24 divided by 6 = 4

The gap is 4 times the retention interval, 400% of it, where 20% to 30% was the aim. This is the revision week before the exam, with a single review. There is a smaller slip in the third line too: the 20% is a share of the retention interval, not of the whole 30 days.

30 divided by 1.2 = 25
0.2 times 25 = 5
30 divided by 1.3 = 23.08
0.3 times 23.08 = 6.92

Revise on day 5 to day 7, which is 25 to 27 October.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable. It uses the right percentage, and revising just before the exam is the habit most of us grew up with. The review feels productive because the exam is close. That is the good feeling this section warns against.

blocks.prompt: A colleague plans reviews for a batch of MBBS students. “Dunlosky and colleagues say: space reviews at 10 to 20% of how long you need to remember. The final examination is 3 years away. So each topic gets its review 3.5 to 7 months after it is taught.” Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: 10% and 20% of 3 years, and then whether the data behind the 10 to 20% reach that far. Take a year as 365 days.

3 times 365 = 1095
0.1 times 1095 = 109.5
0.2 times 1095 = 219

109.5 to 219 days. At about 30 days to a month, that is about 3.7 to 7.3 months, so the colleague’s arithmetic is roughly right.

109.5 divided by 30 = 3.65
219 divided by 30 = 7.3

Dunlosky and colleagues do print this rule. They also carry it to 5 years: “to remember something for 5 years, the learning episodes should be spaced 6 to 12 months apart”. The study behind it, Cepeda and colleagues 2008, stopped at 350 days. There its fitted best gap was 23 days, 7% of the retention interval. The authors say the share must fall as the retention interval grows.

What this does not establish. It does not establish that 3.5 to 7 months is right for 3 years. A fixed 10 to 20% is being carried far past the data, and the data show the share falling. It does not give a better number either: 6% of 3 years would be the same kind of guess. Cepeda and colleagues themselves say only that a review “of at least several months” seems likely to pay off when something must last several years. And one review of trivia facts is not a clinical subject revised for an examination.

What to say to the colleague: keep the long gap, since too long costs less than too short. Earlier, shorter reviews are reasonable too, though no figure here measures them. And do not quote 10 to 20% as if it were measured for 3 years.

blocks.prompt: A coaching advertisement says: “Research shows spacing your study raises what you remember by 64%. Our spaced timetable will raise your university examination marks by 64%.” Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: where 64% came from, and how much it varied inside the same study.

The 64% is Cepeda and colleagues’ figure for recall of trivia facts. It compares the best gap with a gap of zero, with study time the same. The paper also gives it for each retention interval: 10, 59, 111 and 77% for 7, 35, 70 and 350 days.

111 divided by 10 = 11.1

Inside one study, the increase ran from 10% to 111%, an eleven-fold range, depending on when the test came. On the multiple-choice test the per cent increase was 26%, yet the paper’s d there was larger, 1.5 against 1.1 (section 2). A per cent change and a difference in standard deviations can rank the same results differently.

What this does not establish. It does not establish any change in marks. 64% is a per cent change in recall, not in examination marks, and not percentage points. The comparison is against no gap at all, not against however the student studies now. So it is not what a student would gain from switching timetables. The material was trivia facts learned online, not a medical syllabus. And nothing here says this timetable spaces anything well.

What to say: spacing is well supported, and worth using. The 64% is one study’s best case against cramming in one sitting, and it says nothing about marks.
